title: Episode 223: Russia: Catherine the Great, the Winter Palace, and the Bronze Horseman
description:
The extraordinary life of Empress Catherine the Great: arriving in Russia as an impoverished German princess, seizing the imperial throne in a bloodless coup, corresponding with Voltaire, and expanding Russia to the shores of the Black Sea.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we step into the gilded ballrooms and vast imperial expanse of eighteenth-century Russia to explore the life of one of history's most brilliant, audacious, and cultured monarchs: Empress Catherine the Great.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: SOPHIE OF ANHALT-ZERBST: A GERMAN PRINCESS AT THE RUSSIAN COURT
In 1744, an obscure fourteen-year-old German princess named Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst arrived in the freezing grandeur of St. Petersburg, selected by Empress Elizabeth Petrovna to be the bride of the heir to the Russian throne, Grand Duke Peter of Holstein-Gottorp. Arriving with only three dresses and no political influence, Sophie recognized that survival in the treacherous, faction-ridden Russian court required complete assimilation. While her neurotic and immature husband played with toy soldiers and openly voiced his contempt for Russian customs, Sophie stayed up late into the sub-zero winter nights studying Russian grammar, culture, and Orthodox theology, pacing barefoot on stone floors until she contracted severe pneumonia. She converted to the Russian Orthodox Church, adopting the name Ekaterina Alekseyevna—Catherine—and earned the genuine affection of the Russian clergy, nobility, and palace guards. Her marriage was an unmitigated disaster: Peter ignored her for eighteen lonely years, during which Catherine read deeply in the political philosophy of Montesquieu, Tacitus, and Voltaire, quietly preparing her mind for the staggering destiny she intended to seize.  Young Sophie's German tutor in Stettin had instilled in her a love of French literature, but upon arriving in Russia she realized that only by outdoing the native Russians in Orthodoxy and patriotism could she ever secure her place at court.  Grand Duke Peter's childish games included court-martialing and hanging a pet rat that had chewed on one of his toy soldiers, an incident that convinced Catherine that her husband was utterly unfit to govern the Russian Empire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE COUP OF 1762: THE EMPRESS TAKES THE THRONE
When Empress Elizabeth died in January 1762, Catherine's husband ascended the throne as Tsar Peter III. Within six erratic months, Peter alienated every pillar of Russian society: he abruptly withdrew Russian troops from the Seven Years' War on the brink of defeating Prussia, returned all conquered lands to Frederick the Great out of personal idol-worship, and threatened to divorce and imprison Catherine. Seeing her moment, Catherine formed an alliance with the elite Izmailovsky and Preobrazhensky Guards regiments, led by her dashing lover, Grigory Orlov. In the early morning hours of June 28, 1762, Catherine was awakened at the Peterhof palace by Alexei Orlov, who whispered, 'Everything is ready; you must come.' Dressing in the green uniform of the Guards and mounting an astride stallion, Catherine rode into St. Petersburg surrounded by cheering regiments. The Senate and Holy Synod unanimously proclaimed her sovereign ruler of Russia. Peter III was arrested, forced to sign an unconditional abdication, and died eight days later under mysterious circumstances at Ropsha estate. At the age of thirty-three, a German-born outsider with not a single drop of Russian blood had seized the imperial crown of the Romanov dynasty.  The five Orlov brothers possessed enormous physical strength and popularity among the Guards regiments, distributing thousands of rubles in taverns across St. Petersburg to ensure the soldiers' unwavering loyalty to Catherine on the day of the coup.  On the day of the coup, Catherine was escorted by thousands of soldiers who pinned oak sprigs to their hats, marching through St. Petersburg to the Cathedral of Our Lady of Kazan where the Archbishop administered the oath of fealty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE PHILOSOPHE EMPRESS AND THE WINTER PALACE
Catherine envisioned herself as an enlightened despot—a philosopher-monarch who would govern according to reason, law, and education while preserving absolute imperial authority. She began a famous personal correspondence with the intellectual giants of the French Enlightenment, exchanging witty, philosophical letters with Voltaire, who hailed her as 'The Star of the North'. When French authorities banned Denis Diderot's monumental Encyclopédie, Catherine offered to publish it in Russia, and when Diderot fell into financial ruin, she purchased his library for a fortune while paying him an annual salary to remain its custodian in Paris. In 1767, Catherine drafted the Nakaz, or Great Instruction—a groundbreaking legal treatise drawing heavily on Beccaria and Montesquieu that condemned torture, championed the rule of law, and proposed modern civic rights. She convened a grand Legislative Commission of over five hundred deputies representing nobles, merchants, Cossacks, and free peasants to draft a modern legal code. Simultaneously, she turned the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg into a world capital of culture, founding the Hermitage Museum by acquiring thousands of masterpieces by Rembrandt, Raphael, Titian, and Rubens.  Voltaire was so enchanted by Catherine's intellect and political patronage that he referred to her as his 'Northern Semiramis', defending her policies in French intellectual salons against critics of Russian autocracy.  Catherine's passion for classical art and architecture transformed St. Petersburg into a neoclassical jewel, commissioning Giacomo Quarenghi and Charles Cameron to design magnificent marble palaces, colonnades, and public squares.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PUGACHEV REBELLION: THE GHOST OF THE TSAR ALONG THE VOLGA
Catherine's enlightened dreams of reforming serfdom were shattered in 1773 by the most terrifying peasant uprising in Russian history: the Pugachev Rebellion. A charismatic Don Cossack named Emelyan Pugachev declared that he was Tsar Peter III, miraculously saved from Catherine's assassins, promising freedom from serfdom, exemption from taxes, and the extermination of the landlord class. Thousands of oppressed serfs, Ural factory workers, Bashkirs, and Kalmyks flocked to his banner, burning down noble manors, hanging landlords, and butchering imperial garrisons across thousands of square miles between the Volga and Ural rivers. The rebellion sent shockwaves through the St. Petersburg court, threatening the very foundations of the Russian state. Catherine dispatched her finest generals to crush the revolt with overwhelming military force. Pugachev was betrayed, captured, brought to Moscow in an iron cage, and publicly executed in Red Square in 1775. The trauma of the revolt taught Catherine a sobering political lesson: her throne rested entirely upon the loyalty of the Russian nobility. In 1785, she issued the Charter to the Nobility, cementing their privileges and giving them absolute authority over their millions of serfs.  Pugachev's peasant army swelled to over twenty-five thousand fighters, establishing an alternative imperial court complete with fake ministers and issuing decrees in the name of Peter III that abolished serfdom across the Volga basin.  The Pugachev rebellion forced Catherine to abandon her idealistic plans for serf emancipation, recognizing that attempting to liberate the peasantry would provoke a violent aristocratic backlash that would cost her the imperial throne.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: PRINCE POTEMKIN, THE CONQUEST OF CRIMEA, AND NOVOROSSIYA
The greatest partnership of Catherine's life was with Prince Grigory Potemkin—a brilliant, one-eyed military strategist, administrator, and the love of her life. Together, they executed the audacious 'Greek Project', aimed at pushing back the Ottoman Empire and establishing Russian dominance over the Black Sea. In two victorious wars against the Ottoman Turks, Russian armies under Field Marshal Alexander Suvorov won legendary victories at Izmail and Rymnik. In 1783, Potemkin achieved the crowning triumph of Catherine's reign: the bloodless annexation of the Crimean Peninsula, securing an ice-free southern outlet to the Mediterranean. Potemkin transformed the barren southern steppe—christened Novorossiya, or New Russia—founding the fortress port of Sevastopol, the Black Sea naval fleet, and the vibrant commercial cities of Odessa, Kherson, and Ekaterinoslav. In 1787, Catherine made an imperial progress through Crimea, accompanied by Holy Roman Emperor Joseph II, marveling at the newly built cities, flourishing vineyards, and formidable naval fleet created out of thin air by Potemkin's administrative genius.  Potemkin's military reforms eliminated useless ornamental wigs and tight uniforms for Russian soldiers, replacing them with practical, loose-fitting green tunics and comfortable leather boots designed for brutal winter campaigns in the Crimean steppe.  Potemkin's conquest of the Crimea opened the vast fertile black-earth steppes of Ukraine to agricultural cultivation, turning Russia into the preeminent grain exporter of continental Europe within a generation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SMALLPOX INOCULATION: AN ACT OF IMPERIAL BRAVERY
Amidst her political and military triumphs, Catherine performed an act of personal courage that saved millions of Russian lives. In the eighteenth century, smallpox was the deadliest scourge in Europe, claiming hundreds of thousands of lives annually and disfiguring millions, including Catherine's husband Peter. When an English physician named Thomas Dimsdale arrived in St. Petersburg promoting the controversial practice of variolation—inoculating patients with live smallpox matter from an infected blister—Russian doctors and clergy vehemently opposed it as dangerous and ungodly. Knowing that ordinary Russians would never accept the procedure without an undeniable example, Catherine secretly summoned Dimsdale to the Winter Palace in October 1768 and insisted that she be inoculated first. If she died, Dimsdale was provided with swift post-horses to flee the country. Catherine endured a week of fever and pustules in seclusion before emerging fully recovered and permanently immune. She then had her son Paul inoculated. Her fearless example triggered nationwide inoculation campaigns across Russia, making Catherine a pioneering champion of public health and modern medical science.  Catherine's courage during the smallpox inoculation silenced domestic skeptics, prompting grand dukes, court ladies, and provincial governors to line up by the thousands to receive the life-saving treatment from Doctor Dimsdale.  When Doctor Dimsdale completed the royal inoculations without complication, Catherine rewarded him with a hereditary barony, a lavish pension of five hundred pounds a year, and a diamond-encrusted portrait of the empress.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BRONZE HORSEMAN AND THE IMPERIAL HORIZON
To honor the founder of St. Petersburg and legitimize her own reign, Catherine commissioned the French sculptor Étienne Maurice Falconet to create an equestrian statue of Peter the Great. The monument, unveiled in 1782 in Senate Square, depicted Peter rearing his steed on the edge of a precipice, trampling a serpent of treason, his outstretched hand pointing westward toward Europe. The pedestal was carved from the colossal Thunder Stone—a single four-hundred-ton granite boulder dragged six miles through Finnish bogs by hundreds of men using ingenious brass ball bearings. On the stone, Catherine inscribed a simple, magnificent dedication in Latin and Russian: 'To Peter the First, Catherine the Second, 1782.' When Catherine died in November 1796 at the age of sixty-seven, she had governed for thirty-four glorious years. She had added over two hundred thousand square miles to the Russian Empire, crushed the Ottoman Empire, partitioned Poland, founded dozens of cities, and established Russia as a premier cultural and military superpower of the Western world.  Falconet worked for twelve years on the Bronze Horseman, using Russian cavalry officers leaping their horses onto an artificial wooden mound to capture the dynamic tension of Peter's rearing steed in bronze.  Alexander Pushkin later immortalized Falconet's monument in his masterpiece poem 'The Bronze Horseman', depicting the stone idol galloping through the flooded streets of St. Petersburg as an eternal symbol of Russia's untamed imperial destiny.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our European journey moves south into Central Europe to explore the Habsburg heartland with Episode 224: Austria Part 1—Maria Theresa, the Pragmatic Sanction, and the Mother of an Empire. Until then, stay curious.
